newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Holzmann falls despite '96 break-even.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Holzmann falls despite '96 break-even.

text.p: Shares in Germany's largest construction group, Philipp Holzmann AG, fell against the market trend on Friday despite a management report confirming earlier forecasts that it would break even in 1996.

The shares fell two marks to 421 on an otherwise strong German bourse after Holzmann said in a preliminary profit statement that construction output in 1996 was just under 14 billion marks, down from 14.1 billion marks in 1995.
Holzmann shares have risen nearly a third in the last three months on hopes that fellow building group Hochtief AG will be allowed to increase its 20 percent stake in the group to 35 percent.
In its statement, Holzmann said the estimated 1996 break-even took into account charges of one billion marks ($609 million) resulting from writedowns on share stakes, operating losses and provisions.
They follow the 458 million marks of write-downs on real estate projects charged in 1995.

Construction analysts, while expressing some relief after 1995 losses of 443 million marks, said the continued weakness of the German construction market meant there was no guarantee that the write-downs were finally over.

"I still can't see any light at the end of the tunnel for the building sector, in 1997 at least," said Karin Brinkmann, analyst at Munich-based Bayerische Hypotheken und Wechsel-Bank. She still saw Holzmann stock as an "underperformer".
Holzmann chief Lothar Mayer earlier said the group would continue its restructuring in 1997, cutting its workforce in Germany by a further 10 percent this year.
"(The restructuring) will lead to better working processes and cost-savings that will markedly improve the operating result," Mayer said in a statement.
Incoming orders totalled just under 16 billion marks, up from 15.6 billion marks, and orders on hand totalled more than 15 billion marks, up from 13.6 billion marks.
Holzmann said its financial situation had significantly improved in 1996, with short-term cash and security balances rising to more than 2.5 billion marks from 1.7 billion.
Holzmann shares came under pressure late last year following a spate of reports, all denied, that the group had liquidity problems which were putting its bank credit lines in danger.
Mayer said that its marketing of real estate projects was going ahead of plan, with around two-thirds of projected real estate sales for 1996 and 1997 already secured.

There is however a continued mood of pessimism surrounding German building stocks because of the weak outlook for demand and prices in the domestic market, where infrastructure investment is estimated to be falling.

Analysts are eager to see a mooted link-up with Hochtief, under which the two groups would collaborate more closely on construction projects and Hochtief management would have a stronger say in the running of Holzmann.
Previous attempts by Hochtief to increase its interest in Holzmann have been vetoed by German cartel authorities, but new hearings are due to start on the matter in early April.
